newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Chemical trader pleads guilty over trades.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Chemical trader pleads guilty over trades.

text.p: Victor Gomez, formerly Chemical Bank's principal trader in Mexican pesos, pleaded guilty Thursday to making unauthorized trades that resulted in a $70 million loss to the bank in 1994.
Gomez, 35, pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court to a 13-count indictment charging him with bank fraud and making false entries in bank records.
He faces a possible maximum sentence of 30 years on each count and fines of $1 million on each count.
U.S. District Judge Michael Mukasey set a sentencing date of December 13.
Gomez had been arrested on March 20 by Scotland Yard at his home is Chesham, outside of London.
The indictment, returned by a Manhattan federal jury on March 13, charged that in November and December 1994, Gomez took unauthorized positions in Mexican pesos exceeding $200 million.
He admitting hiding the positions by entering fictitious offsetting trades into Chemical's computer systems.
The secret positions caused the bank to lose about $70 million when the peso was suddenly devalued on Dec. 20, 1994 and in its subsequent further fall.
In pleading guilty, Gomez said that he had intended for the trades to be profitable.
"At no time did I intend to victimize Chemical Bank," he told the judge.
Gomez's trading was discovered by Chemical Bank at the end of December 1994 and it publicly announced the losses on January 3, 1995.

Gomez' compensation was determined in part by the profits or losses generated by his trading. During 1994, the majority of the trading he reported was in Mexican pesos. His base salary that year was about $85,000, but the bank approved a bonus of $105,000 based substantially on his trading in pesos.

He was fired in late December 1994 and did not receive the bonus. Gomez had been a vice-president of the bank and was employed in its Foreign Exchange Trading Department in New York. From May to December 1994 he was the principal trader in that department for Mexican pesos. Chemical has since merged with Chase Manhattan Corp.

The indictment also charges that Gomez entered into another series of unauthorized transactions in which he committed Chemical to guarantee another financial institution that it would convert Mexican pesos into dollars, if for any reason the Mexican government barred such transactions.
He is also charged with making unauthorized investments of funds in Chemical's peso account in Mexico City.
Gomez was released on a $250,000 personal recognizance bond secured by equity in his brother-in-law's house.
